reading.synopsis: Elderly country storekeeper Edna Berthelson makes a secretive weekly business trip alone in her pickup truck, exploiting an inexplicable personal ability to shift into a branching post-nuclear-war 'ahead' where a small colony of survivors is desperately assembling a salvaged Army rocket to escape a dying, radioactive Earth for Venus. She sells them supplies at ruinously exploitative prices, having discovered she alone can make the crossing, and has quietly amassed a small fortune in money the colonists themselves regard as worthless. When her grandson Jackie stows away to see where she goes, he falls through mid-transition and is left behind unharmed in the ordinary present, never learning her secret. Once the colonists announce they have finally gathered enough supplies to launch and no longer need her, Mrs. Berthelson, coldly furious at losing her only market, uses her power to browse among the countless branching timelines and deliberately selects — from the several available outcomes, including successful escape — the one specific 'ahead' in which the ship's launch fails catastrophically and crashes, ensuring the survivors remain trapped, injured, and dependent on her for supplies indefinitely.

structure.form: short story in three interwoven movements: Edna's secretive weekly trip and the stowaway grandson subplot, the colony's desperate final preparations for launch, and Edna's furious, deliberate selection of a failure-timeline once her market threatens to disappear
movements: Edna Berthelson prepares for her secretive weekly trading trip while her grandson Jackie, curious about her long-guarded 'find,' secretly stows away in the truck bed.

In a branching post-war future, a small colony of Bay Area survivors is assembling a salvaged Army rocket for a desperate escape to Venus, entirely dependent on Edna's weekly supply runs for the parts and materials they cannot produce themselves.

Learning the colonists no longer need her because their final supply load has arrived, Edna -- having lost Jackie mid-transition without him ever discovering her secret -- coldly browses the branching timelines available to her and deliberately selects the one in which the ship's launch fails and crashes, trapping the colonists as her captive market indefinitely.
structure.point_of_view: third person, alternating between Edna's businesslike, faintly sinister interiority and the colonists' (Tellman, Crowley, Flannery, Patricia Shelby) desperate hope for escape, so the reader shares the colonists' relief at finally being free of her exploitative arrangement right up until Edna's final, chosen sabotage.
structure.central_device: A branching-timeline power used not for adventure or heroism but for coldly rational commercial advantage, so that a monopolist's ordinary economic self-interest (preserving a captive customer base) becomes, when paired with literal control over which future actually occurs, an act of engineered, permanent atrocity.

characters.name: Edna Berthelson
characters.note: Her ordinary, small-business rationality and rigid inherited business ethics ('her father's rules') are never abandoned even as she commits what amounts to mass murder by timeline-selection -- the story frames her atrocity entirely within the register of ruthless but mundane commercial self-interest rather than as supernatural malice.

characters.name: Jackie
characters.note: His stowaway curiosity and subsequent unexplained fall back into the ordinary present frames the story's opening with childlike wonder, contrasting sharply with the coldly transactional reality he never gets to see.

characters.name: Flannery, Crowley, Patricia Shelby, Masterson, Tellman
characters.note: Given full sympathetic interiority -- exhaustion, hope, dark gallows humor, hunger for real coffee and a decent meal -- their belief that they have finally secured their freedom from Edna's exploitation makes the story's final reveal an act of narrative cruelty directed as much at the reader as at them.

settings.name: Walnut Creek, 1965 (Edna's present)
settings.note: An ordinary, prosperous suburban California setting, its mundane comforts (apricot orchards, a swank tavern, seventy-five-mile-an-hour Chryslers) juxtaposed sharply against the catastrophe unfolding just one 'ahead' away.

settings.name: The post-Blast colony camp
settings.note: A desperate settlement of survivors sheltering in the ruins of a mountain range near incinerated San Francisco, their salvaged Army rocket representing their only hope of leaving a dying, radioactive Earth.

motifs: A monopolist's exploitation of a genuinely captive customer base, literalized through control over branching timelines rather than merely economic circumstance
Ordinary small-business ethics and rigor applied without any moral adjustment to a context of literal life-and-death stakes
A child's innocent curiosity about a family secret that turns out to conceal atrocity rather than mere eccentricity
A desperate escape narrative's hope deliberately, coldly foreclosed by an external agent's self-interest rather than by any inherent flaw in the escape plan itself
reading.significance: The story's power comes from refusing to give Edna Berthelson any trace of supernatural villainy or cosmic malice — she is simply an elderly small-town businesswoman applying her father's rigid commercial principles to an extraordinary power, and her final act of sabotage is presented in exactly the same flat, procedural tone as her routine inventory-checking. This makes 'Captive Market' one of Dick's clearest early parables about capitalism divorced from any moral limit: given genuinely unique market power (here, literal control over which future occurs), the story suggests, a purely rational actor optimizing for continued profit will make exactly the choice Edna makes, with no larger ideology or evil required, only the ordinary, unexamined assumption that a good customer is worth preserving by any means necessary.
reading.closing_note: Crowley's repeated, increasingly desperate insistence -- 'We'll get away... we've got to get away!' -- closes the story on a hope the reader already knows is false, since Edna has already chosen, with cold deliberation, the specific branch of the future in which that hope fails.

distinctive_terms.label: Black
distinctive_terms.note: The recurring 'black ash' of the devastated Earth is the story's dominant visual motif for the colonists' entrapment.

distinctive_terms.label: Father
distinctive_terms.note: Edna's repeated invocation of her father's business principles frames her atrocity as inherited commercial ethics rather than personal malice.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a branching-timeline power used not for adventure but for coldly rational commercial advantage, including the deliberate selection of a specific catastrophic future to preserve a captive customer base
a monopolist trading partner's ordinary economic self-interest curdling into an act of engineered, permanent sabotage the instant her customers threaten to become independent of her

open_questions: Is there documented commentary from Dick on his choice to render Edna Berthelson's atrocity in such flatly mundane, small-business terms rather than as cosmic villainy?
Is this story ever discussed by critics as an early, unusually direct critique of monopolistic capitalism, given how precisely Edna's reasoning tracks ordinary market-preservation logic?
What became of Jackie's fall back into the ordinary present -- is there any indication the story intends for him eventually to learn what his grandmother actually does on her weekly trips?
